steps.title: Rules are data: a YAML file, not code
steps.plain: A data engineer describes the checks for the orders dataset in a YAML file: seven rules, each with a severity (error or warn) and an action (quarantine the bad rows, stop the load, or just alert). No Python, no SQL. The file also names the engine that runs the checks (dq_engine), and that one line is the binding: the pipeline never imports Deequ or Great Expectations directly. Today's bronze batch has 50,012 orders.

steps.title: Loaded into the metadata DB, compiled by the port
steps.plain: A loader validates the YAML and writes it to the metadata database: one row per rule in dq_rule, and the dataset row with the engine binding and a fingerprint of the rules (c9850a44be01). Every run records which fingerprint it checked against, so 'which rules were in force on 27 Oct?' has an answer. The port compiles each rule for the bound engine. Both compilations are shown: the same seven rules as Spark SQL, and as Deequ checks. Deequ has no referential-integrity rule, so the port routes DQ-07 to Spark SQL: the adapter declares what it supports instead of failing.
steps.code:
loader: validate YAML -> INSERT INTO dataset_master, dq_rule; fingerprint = sha256(canonical rules)

-- DQ-01 is_complete
SELECT avg(CASE WHEN customer_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1D ELSE 0D END) AS metric FROM bronze_orders   -- pass if = 1.0
-- DQ-02 is_unique
SELECT sum(CASE WHEN n = 1 THEN n ELSE 0 END) / sum(n) AS metric FROM (SELECT order_id, count(*) n FROM bronze_orders GROUP BY order_id)   -- pass if = 1.0
-- DQ-03 is_non_negative
SELECT avg(CASE WHEN amount IS NULL OR amount >= 0 THEN 1D ELSE 0D END) AS metric FROM bronze_orders   -- pass if = 1.0
-- DQ-04 is_contained_in
SELECT avg(CASE WHEN country IS NULL OR country IN ('IN', 'US', 'GB', 'AE', 'SG') THEN 1D ELSE 0D END) AS metric FROM bronze_orders   -- pass if = 1.0
-- DQ-05 completeness_at_least
SELECT avg(CASE WHEN coupon IS NOT NULL THEN 1D ELSE 0D END) AS metric FROM bronze_orders   -- pass if >= 0.05
-- DQ-06 row_count_between
SELECT count(*) AS metric FROM bronze_orders   -- pass if between 40000 and 60000
-- DQ-07 references
SELECT avg(CASE WHEN bronze_orders.customer_id IS NULL OR r.customer_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1D ELSE 0D END) AS metric FROM bronze_orders LEFT JOIN customers r ON bronze_orders.customer_id = r.customer_id   -- pass if = 1.0
compiled.deequ (same rules, if the binding said d:
VerificationSuite(spark).onData(bronze_orders)
  .addCheck(Check(spark, CheckLevel.Error, 'DQ-01').isComplete('customer_id'))
  .addCheck(Check(spark, CheckLevel.Error, 'DQ-02').isUnique('order_id'))
  .addCheck(Check(spark, CheckLevel.Error, 'DQ-03').isNonNegative('amount'))
  .addCheck(Check(spark, CheckLevel.Warning, 'DQ-04').isContainedIn('country', ['IN', 'US', 'GB', 'AE', 'SG']))
  .addCheck(Check(spark, CheckLevel.Warning, 'DQ-05').hasCompleteness('coupon', lambda x: x >= 0.05))
  .addCheck(Check(spark, CheckLevel.Error, 'DQ-06').hasSize(lambda x: 40000 <= x <= 60000))
  # DQ-07 references: Deequ has no referential check -> the port routes it to spark_sql
  .run()

steps.title: Run with the Spark SQL adapter: results, quarantine, alerts
steps.plain: The pipeline calls the port; the binding says spark_sql. 5 of 7 rules fail, and each failure does what its action says. Rows that break an error rule (no customer, a duplicate order delivered again, a negative amount) go to quarantine with the rule IDs (232 rows). Warnings (country 'Ind', customers missing from the customer table) raise alerts but keep the rows. The row count is in range, so the load is not stopped: 49,780 rows published to silver. Checks took 2793 ms.

results = dq_port.run(rules, 'bronze_orders')        # binding: spark_sql
apply_actions(results)   # quarantine | stop | alert, per rule

steps.title: Change one line: the same rules on Deequ
steps.plain: The binding changes from spark_sql to deequ, in the YAML and therefore in the metadata DB. No pipeline code changes. The port builds a Deequ VerificationSuite from the same rows: 6 rules run on Deequ, and DQ-07 (referential integrity) is routed to Spark SQL because the Deequ adapter declares it cannot do that. Every verdict agrees (yes), and 6 of the 6 metrics Deequ computed match the Spark SQL ones to six significant digits. One lesson from building the port: Deequ's 'uniqueness' means 'share of rows whose value appears exactly once', so the Spark SQL adapter computes exactly that, not 'distinct values / rows'. A port is only swappable if every adapter means the same thing by each rule. Running both adapters side by side also caught a bug in our own: the first Spark SQL adapter averaged decimal literals, and Spark rounded the metrics (0.996 instead of 0.99600096). It now averages doubles, and that comparison is kept as a contract test for the port.

results = dq_port.run(rules, 'bronze_orders')   # same call

steps.title: Profile the data before writing rules
steps.plain: Deequ's column profiler reads the table once and describes every column: type, completeness, approximate distinct count, and for numbers the minimum, maximum and mean. It took 1520 ms for 50,012 rows. The profile already shows the problems: customer_id is not 100% complete, amount has a negative minimum, and the country histogram includes 'Ind', which is not an ISO code. Profile first, then write rules: it is cheaper than guessing.

steps.title: Let Deequ suggest rules; a person decides
steps.plain: Deequ's suggestion runner proposes 10 rules from the data itself (complete columns, value ranges, allowed values). Useful, but they describe today's data, not the business: here it suggests that customer_id may have up to 1% missing values, and that country may be 'Ind'. Accepted blindly, those rules would bless today's bugs. So suggestions are written to a draft YAML in a pull request, labelled proposed, and a person accepts or rejects each one. Suggestions touch columns with no rule yet: placed_at. Nothing here changes a rule automatically.

steps.title: Five days of metrics, and the day the count fell
steps.plain: Every run stores its metrics in Deequ's metrics repository (5 Size metrics stored, one per day). An anomaly check compares today's row count with the history: fail if it fell by more than half since the last run. It needs at least one previous run, so it starts on the second day. Days 23–26 Oct are normal (about 50,000 orders). On 27 Oct only 19,812 rows arrived: the anomaly check fails, and so does DQ-06 (row count between 40,000 and 60,000), whose action is stop. Silver keeps yesterday's data instead of publishing a third of today's. A fixed range catches the obvious; the anomaly check also catches a drop inside the range, because it learns from history.
logs: 2026-10-27: 19,812 rows; anomaly check FAILED: size fell more than 50% vs the previous run; DQ-06 → stop: silver not updated

steps.title: A new dataset, onboarded with nine lines of YAML
steps.plain: The CRM team wants checks on their customers table. The whole change is one new YAML file, reviewed as a pull request: three rules, bound to Deequ. The loader adds it to the metadata DB, the same port runs it, the same actions apply. No pipeline code, no new job. The tier rule catches three rows written as 'gold' instead of 'Gold'; it is a warning, so the owner is alerted and the rows are kept. This is what metadata-driven, low-code data quality means: the engine is built once, and each dataset is a file.
